Chapter 2: Building a Culture of Secrecy and Fear
As the company grew, something subtle but important started to change. What used to feel like a place where everyone was working together, united by a common goal, slowly shifted into a world where trust was rare. New hires came in, full of excitement and hope, drawn by the idea that they could help transform healthcare. But pretty soon, they found themselves lost in a maze of closed doors and hushed conversations.
The founder, now in the spotlight, built a close-knit group of loyal followers. If you weren’t part of that inner circle, information was handed out only on a need-to-know basis—and even then, it was often vague or just plain misleading. The message was loud and clear: curiosity could get you into trouble, and being loyal meant keeping your head down and your mouth shut.
And if you did start asking questions? The consequences came quickly. Some folks were suddenly left out of the loop, their work picked apart for any hint of disloyalty. Others were shown the door, often without much explanation. The company’s legal team got a reputation for being tough—almost ruthless—making sure everyone understood that speaking out could cost you, big time.
Take one engineer, for example. They joined the company, fired up by its bold mission. But it didn’t take long to realize that the tech just wasn’t living up to the hype. Any attempt to address these problems met stiff resistance. When this person tried to raise their concerns, what happened? Meetings behind closed doors, subtle threats, and a growing sense of isolation. It was obvious—honesty wasn’t welcome.
But this secrecy wasn’t just about keeping company secrets safe. It was about keeping a tight grip on the narrative, both inside and outside those walls. Employees were constantly reminded how important it was to keep things confidential. Even casual chats felt risky, and rumors of surveillance floated through the office. The message? Trust no one—not even your teammates.
The pressure to deliver only made things worse. Deadlines were short, and the whole world seemed to be watching. Managers pushed teams to meet impossible goals, ignoring what the technology could actually deliver. And when things went wrong, the instinct wasn’t to fix it—it was to cover it up.
For a lot of people, the stress just got to be too much. Some decided they couldn’t stick it out and left, unwilling to betray their own values. Others stayed, hoping for change, but found themselves stuck in a system that rewarded silence and punished honesty. Speaking up simply cost too much.
Meanwhile, outside the company, everything looked perfect. The founder kept winning over investors and the media, spinning setbacks as just minor bumps in the road. Hardly anyone questioned the story, and even when they did, getting real answers was almost impossible. The board—packed with big names—rarely challenged anything.
